name: Potato
perishability: Semi-perishable. Months in cold storage; weeks at room temperature.
summary: A one-harvest, cold-storage commodity. Almost all of the crop is dug in the Indo-Gangetic plains in January–March and loaded into cold stores, then released through the year. Prices climb steadily from June and peak in October–November, just before the new crop.

key_numbers.label: Production 2024-25
key_numbers.note: Final; up from 570.5 lakh t in 2023-24

key_numbers.label: Cold storage
key_numbers.note: of India's ~40 million t cold-store capacity is used for potato

global: India is the world's second-largest potato producer after China. Exports (mostly to Nepal, Sri Lanka, Oman, Malaysia) are a few lakh tonnes a year.

rows.hubs: Agra, Firozabad, Aligarh, Hathras, Mainpuri, Kannauj, Farrukhabad
Hooghly, Purba & Paschim Bardhaman, Bankura, Paschim Medinipur
Assam, Haryana, Jharkhand, Karnataka (kharif), Himachal (seed), Meghalaya

belts.name: Agra belt
belts.note: Densest cluster of cold stores in India.

belts.name: Farrukhabad–Kannauj
belts.note: Major table-potato supply to North and East India.

belts.name: Hooghly–Bardhaman
belts.note: Feeds Odisha, Jharkhand, Assam and the North-East; West Bengal sometimes restricts movement out of state.

belts.name: Deesa
belts.note: Processing potatoes for chips and fries (PepsiCo, McCain, Balaji).

belts.name: Jalandhar seed belt
belts.note: Certified seed potatoes for UP, Bihar and West Bengal, grown in a low-aphid window.

seasons.name: Rabi (plains)
seasons.region: UP, WB, Bihar, Punjab, Gujarat, MP
seasons.note: Loaded into cold stores Feb–Mar; released Apr–Nov.

seasons.name: Kharif (plateau)
seasons.note: Fresh potatoes for South India in autumn.

lean_season: October–November: cold-store stocks are thinning and the new crop has not arrived.

climate.v: Tubers form best at 15–20 °C; night temperatures above ~22 °C slow tuber formation and above 30 °C stop it.
Short winter days in the plains favour tuber formation.
Frost kills foliage; long foggy spells trigger late blight epidemics.
Loose, well-drained sandy loam, pH 5.2–6.5 (tolerates up to ~7.5).
Needs steady moisture at tuber bulking; excess water at harvest causes rot in storage.

weather_risks.impact: Can destroy foliage within days and cut yields sharply.

weather_risks.risk: Cyclone or late rains at planting
weather_risks.impact: Waterlogged fields delay or force replanting.
weather_risks.example: Cyclone Jawad (Dec 2021) and Michaung (Dec 2023) rains hit Bengal planting.

weather_risks.impact: Wet tubers go into storage and rot.
Shortens the bulking period and cuts yield.

pests.name: Late blight
pests.impact: The defining risk: rapid foliage collapse in cool, humid weather.

pests.name: Black scurf / common scab
pests.impact: Blemishes lower the grade and price.

pests.name: Viruses (PVY, PLRV)
pests.impact: Seed degeneration; why seed comes from low-aphid areas.

pests.name: Bacterial wilt (brown rot)
pests.impact: Wilting and rotting tubers in warm areas.

pests.name: Golden cyst nematode
pests.impact: Quarantine pest in the Nilgiris and parts of the hills.

postharvest.storage: Table and seed: 2–4 °C, 90–95% RH. Processing grade: 10–12 °C with a sprout suppressant (CIPC) to avoid sugar build-up.
postharvest.shelf_ambient: 2–3 months in well-ventilated heaps if cured; tubers sprout and shrink in summer.
postharvest.chilling: Below ~8 °C starch turns into sugar ('cold sweetening'), which makes chips and fries brown. Table potatoes tolerate it.

loss.detail: Harvest-to-retail loss. Cold-store weight loss of 2–4% is extra.

practices: Curing for 10–15 days in shade heals skin before cold storage.
Cold-store rent is charged per bag per season and is notified by state governments in UP and West Bengal.
Cold-store owners often finance farmers and traders against stored stock.
Bags of 50 kg (jute or HDPE). Big chip makers contract-farm specific varieties.

steps.what: Dug by hand or digger in Jan–Mar; cured and bagged.
Farmer or trader stores in a village or town cold store; receipts double as collateral.
Stock leaves the cold store in phases from April; traders sell in Agra, Kolkata and Farrukhabad markets.
Trucks to Maharashtra, the South, Odisha, Assam and the North-East.
Terminal markets → vendors, modern retail and quick commerce.

supply_chain.packaging: 50 kg jute or HDPE bags; mostly unrefrigerated trucks after release from cold store.

markets.name: Agra APMC
markets.role: Cold-store hub; North India price setter.

markets.name: Farrukhabad (Satanpur) APMC
markets.role: One of the largest potato markets.

varieties.name: Kufri Pukhraj
varieties.note: Most widely grown table variety; early maturing.

varieties.name: Kufri Jyoti, Kufri Bahar, Kufri Badshah, Kufri Chandramukhi
Kufri Chipsona-1/3/4, Kufri FryoM
varieties.note: ICAR-CPRI processing varieties for chips and fries.

varieties.name: Lady Rosetta, Atlantic, FC-5
varieties.note: Contract-farmed chipping varieties (FC-5 is PepsiCo's variety and the subject of a long plant-variety rights dispute).

varieties.name: Red potatoes (Kufri Sindhuri, Kufri Lalit)
varieties.note: Preferred in East India and Bengal.

trade.exports: A few lakh tonnes a year to Nepal, Sri Lanka, Oman, Malaysia, UAE.

policy.what: West Bengal restricted potato trucks leaving the state to hold local prices down, disrupting supply to Odisha, Jharkhand and Assam.
States notify cold-store rents (UP, WB) and run market intervention in gluts.
Covered under Operation Greens (TOP) for freight and storage subsidies.

history.what: Retail ₹30–40/kg; West Bengal blocked out-of-state movement.
Glut: farm prices ₹1–3/kg; potatoes abandoned in Agra cold stores.
Retail ₹40–50/kg; government allowed imports of 10 lakh t at a reduced 10% duty.
Retail ₹40–50/kg after a weak 2023-24 crop; Bengal movement curbs.

signals: Cold-store loading in March and remaining stock in Aug–Oct (UP and WB horticulture departments, cold-store associations).
Planting area and weather in Oct–Nov in UP, WB and Bihar.
West Bengal government orders on inter-state movement.
Processor contracts and chip-variety acreage in Gujarat and MP.
business: Storage economics drive everything: farmers and traders decide in March whether to sell or store based on rent and expected October prices.
Processing demand (chips, fries, flakes) is growing faster than table demand and pays premiums for specific varieties and sugar levels.
Seed potato quality is a large, under-served market; certified seed covers only a small part of planting needs.
Spreads between Agra/Kolkata and southern markets reflect freight and are fairly stable, making potato good for multi-city sourcing.
